turns.prompt: Could you explain, in some detail, how ocean tides work and why there are usually two a day?
turns.response:
Ocean tides are the regular rise and fall of sea level caused mainly by the Moon’s gravity, with a substantial contribution from the Sun. The key is not simply that the Moon pulls on the ocean: it pulls more strongly on the side of Earth nearest it than on the side farthest away.

Why there are two tidal bulges

Gravity weakens with distance. So the Moon pulls:

  • Most strongly on the side of Earth facing it.
  • A little less strongly on Earth’s center.
  • Least strongly on the opposite side.

To understand tides, compare those pulls with the pull on Earth’s center, because the whole Earth is falling toward the Moon as the two bodies orbit their common center of mass.

On the near side, the ocean is pulled toward the Moon more strongly than Earth’s center is. That difference tends to draw water outward, toward the Moon.

On the far side, Earth’s center is pulled toward the Moon more strongly than the ocean there is. In effect, the Earth is pulled away from that water. Relative to Earth’s center, the water again tends to move outward—this time away from the Moon.

These differences in gravity create a stretching effect along the Earth–Moon direction. In an idealized picture of an Earth entirely covered by ocean, this produces two broad high-water regions: one facing the Moon and one facing away. Between them are lower-water regions.

The far-side bulge is therefore not caused by the Moon repelling water. The Moon attracts everything; the difference in attraction is what matters.

Why that usually means two high tides a day

As Earth rotates, a coastal location passes through the two high-water regions and the two lower-water regions. That gives the basic pattern:

  High tide → low tide → high tide → low tide.

The pattern follows the Moon rather than the Sun. Because the Moon moves along its orbit while Earth rotates, a location takes slightly longer than a solar day to face the Moon again. Consequently, tides generally occur later from one day to the next rather than at fixed clock times.

But the two-bulge picture is a starting point, not a literal map of the ocean. Real tides are enormous, moving waves whose paths and timing are shaped by continents, ocean depth, Earth’s rotation, and the shapes of coastlines and bays. The high tide at your beach need not occur when the Moon is overhead.

What the Sun contributes

The Sun also produces tides. Although its overall gravitational pull on Earth is stronger than the Moon’s, its tide-producing effect is smaller: it is so far away that its pull varies less across Earth.

The solar and lunar tides combine:

  • At new and full Moon, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are approximately aligned. Their tidal effects reinforce one another, producing spring tides—a larger difference between high and low water. “Spring” here has nothing to do with the season.

  • At the first and third quarter phases, the solar and lunar tidal effects partly counteract one another, producing neap tides—a smaller difference between high and low water.

Why “usually” two, rather than always

Different ocean basins respond differently to the tidal forcing. Some coasts have two fairly similar high tides each lunar day, called semidiurnal tides. Others have two noticeably unequal high tides, called mixed tides. Still others have predominantly one high tide and one low tide, called diurnal tides.

The Moon’s and Sun’s changing positions north or south of the equator contribute to these differences, while local ocean geography strongly shapes the result.

In short: the Moon’s uneven gravitational pull creates a two-sided tidal pattern; Earth’s rotation gives most places two encounters with that pattern; and the real ocean’s geography determines how those tides actually appear along each coast.

turns.prompt: Interesting. And why are spring tides bigger than neap tides?
turns.response:
Spring tides have a larger tidal range—the difference between high and low water—because the Moon’s and Sun’s tide-producing effects reinforce each other.

Each body produces a two-sided tidal pattern. What matters is how those patterns line up, not simply whether the Sun and Moon pull in the same direction.

At new Moon, the Sun and Moon are on the same side of Earth. Their tidal patterns align, tending to make high tides higher and low tides lower.

At full Moon, the Sun and Moon are on opposite sides of Earth—but their tidal patterns still align. Because each pattern has a bulge on both sides, their effects reinforce each other here too. Both arrangements produce spring tides.

At first and third quarter Moon, the directions from Earth to the Sun and Moon are roughly at right angles. The Sun’s tidal effect tends to raise water in the regions where the Moon’s effect tends to lower it, and vice versa. They partially cancel, so high tides are less high and low tides less low: neap tides.

They don’t cancel completely because the Moon’s tidal effect is stronger than the Sun’s. Local ocean conditions also affect the timing, so the largest or smallest tidal range can occur somewhat after the corresponding Moon phase.

turns.prompt: One more: how do tide tables get predicted so far in advance?
turns.response:
Tide tables can be predicted far ahead because the main driving forces—the motions of Earth, the Moon, and the Sun—are highly predictable. The harder part is figuring out how the ocean at a particular place responds to those forces.

Turning observations into a prediction

For many locations, the traditional method is called harmonic analysis. Scientists record water levels with a tide gauge, then separate the tidal signal into a collection of repeating cycles, called tidal constituents.

Those cycles reflect different aspects of the astronomical forcing, including:

  • The twice-daily lunar and solar tidal patterns.
  • Daily variations associated with the Moon’s and Sun’s positions relative to the equator.
  • Longer cycles associated with changes in their distances and orbital geometry.

Think of the observed tide as a chord made from many notes. Each constituent has a known astronomical rhythm. Measurements reveal how strongly that “note” appears at the location and where it falls in its cycle—its amplitude and phase.

That local information is essential: a shallow bay might amplify a particular cycle, while another coastline might experience it weakly or with a substantial delay.

Running the cycles forward

Once those amplitudes and phases have been estimated, forecasters project the astronomical cycles forward and add them together. The resulting curve gives predicted water levels; its peaks and troughs give the times and heights of high and low tides.

The spring–neap cycle emerges naturally from this addition: the main lunar and solar components alternately reinforce and partially oppose each other.

Modern predictions can also use numerical ocean models that simulate water movement using ocean depth, coastline shape, and astronomical forcing. These are especially useful where tide-gauge records are limited.

Why the actual water level can differ

A tide table generally predicts the astronomical tide—not everything that can move the sea. Actual water levels also respond to:

  • Winds that push water toward or away from a coast.
  • Atmospheric pressure changes.
  • Storm surges.
  • River flow and changing ocean conditions.

Changes to a harbor or seabed can also alter the local tidal response, making older predictions less accurate.

So the important distinction is this: we can predict the astronomical rhythm years ahead, but we cannot predict the weather’s contribution with the same lead time. A tide table is a reliable forecast of the repeating tidal pattern, not a guarantee of the exact water level on the day.
